newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Pensions burden Yugoslav public finances.
newsitem.headline: Pensions burden Yugoslav public finances.

text.p: Serbia's state Pension Fund has projected spending of around 15 billion dinars ($3 billion) in 1997 but actual demand will be considerably higher because of the soaring numbers of pensioners, economists said on Friday.
Zoran Popov of the Economics Institute told Reuters the fund's ability to meet its pension commitments would depend on how much revenue was collected to finance them.
Popov said the fund, which was not included in the state budget but which was partly paid for by special taxes, cost around 1.1 billion dinars a month in 1996.
The fund's 15 billion dinar estimate included a 1.3 billion dinar deficit from 1996. But Popov calculated the fund owed at least two monthly pensions or 2.2 billion dinars.
Economists warned of a flood of retirements with 100,000 people joining the army of pensioners by early 1997.
"There will be more than 1.5 million pensioners in Serbia alone in 1997, so that one employee will finance one unemployed and one retired person," Popov said.
Montenegro, another constituent republic of Yugoslavia has around 50,000 retired persons, while military pensioners account for another 55,000 to 60,000.
Pensions in Serbia account for one third of the republic's public spending of about 36.5 billion dinars.
Pension funding is mainly from contributions paid equally by workers and employers. Those currently amount to 42.4 percent of the worker's gross salary.
According to some calculations, at least 44 percent of gross wages would be needed to finance pensions in 1997, Aleksandra Posarac of the Institute of Economic Sciences said.
Employee and employer contributions are supplemented by a special tax on telephone calls and a tobacco tax. Recently, a special tax on petrol was also proposed.

"If all goes as planned, Serbia alone needs at least 16 billion dinars to pay pensions at their November 1996 level. In that case, pensions will account for 14-15 percent of the Yugoslav GDP seen at 103 billion dinars in 1997," Posarac said.
Pensions will account for one third of planned public spending in 1997, she added.

"It is very difficult to have a less burdensome pension system when one person employed finances one unemployed and one retired person. In practice, pensions sometimes exceed average wages," Posarac said.
Economists agreed financing pensions was the key problem of Yugoslavia's enormous public spending, seen at 47.5 percent of the 1997 GDP.
"It's a pay-as-you-go scheme. The pension fund is only a form of a bank account. It has no capital of its own," economics professor Jurij Bajec told Reuters.
Bajec insisted the state had to create additional revenues, partly through privatisation, to finance the fund. "If not, a pension scheme like this poses a threat to public finances."
He saw a way out in creating a parallel voluntary social insurance scheme.

Yugoslavia urgently needed to reform its pension system, but any reform would raise the need for even more painful health and education reforms, Pavle Petrovic of the private economic research institute CES-Mecon said.
Popov said the problem was a legacy from the past when the proportion of actively employed to pensioners was four to one and when any shortage of funds was met from external credits.
"The old system was overly generous but if you deny those people their right to a pension, you would create huge social tensions, Popov said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
